detaileddescription.para: This method attempts to calculate the inner radius of the curved-sided quad by talking 1/2 of the perimeter and dividing this measure by the area of the quad.

The procedure is empirically based giving a good match if the quadss are relatively even-sided and have straight edges. Requires further check for the case of the hexahedron, as it is directly borrowed from the Tetrahedron

listitem.para: Pre-multiplies local interpolation function derivative matrix, B, with node coordinates to obtain the Jacobian matrix, J at the desired node point.
The Jacobian matrix J is inverted and multiplied with B to obtain the global interpolation function derivative matrix at the point i (i=0...i=gauss points-1).

sect1.title: Input Arguments
sect1.para: The first argument is a reference to the parent Element object, the second argument is the result matrix, the third argument indicates the gauss point at which the derivative matrix is computed and the fourth argument specifies the degrees of freedom per node, for which the B matrix shall be transformed.

The global interpolation function derivative matrix is returned into the second method argument. The method also returns the determinant of the Jacobian matrix since it is often needed in integration procedures.

detaileddescription.para: As the linear character of the element do not expect high accuracy, one integration point is enough and used in most of the applications (FE, V1 by Zienkewitch).

Because in the local coordinate system, the pyramid is always straight sided, and the derivatives of the interpolation functions are bilinear, variable values computed at integration points can simply be extrapolated to the nodes. This involves the steps:

listitem.para: Compute the interpolation function coefficients for the pyramid which is defined by the one integration point.
For each node point compute the values of the interpolation functions and use these to extrapolate the values of the variables at the nodes.
